source_text: Quid igitur confectum est? Unum esse necessarium de duobus, ut aut confitearis Adam factum bonae esse substantiae, nec naturam eius voluntaria qualitate destructam, et deseras naturale peccatum; aut si illum, ut hactenus opinatus es, naturalium malorum causam esse contenderis, et ipsum pessimae substantiae, atque ad Deum vestrum, id est, tuum et Manichaei, pertinere pronunties.
pass_a_gloss: What therefore has been accomplished? One of two is necessary, that you either confess Adam was made of a good substance, nor was his nature destroyed by a voluntary quality, and you desert a natural sin; or if you shall have contended that he, as you have thus far opined, is the cause of natural evils, you also pronounce him of a worst substance, and belonging to your God, that is, yours and Manichaeus's.

lemmas.lexica: LS necessitas; Blaise vs free choice
Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: What, then, has been established? One of two alternatives is necessary. Either you acknowledge that Adam was made with a good substance, that his nature was not destroyed by a voluntary quality, and you abandon natural sin; or, if you insist as before that he is the cause of natural evils, you must pronounce him too to be of an utterly evil substance and to belong to your god—that is, yours and Mani’s.

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
